transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-02-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 1:12
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE); Maya Singh (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions); Liam O'Connor (Nimble Head of AI); Priya Mehta (Nimble SRE); Carla Ruiz (Nimble PM); Daniel Park (Nimble Backend)

Summary: Kickoff for POC harness integration. Primary goals: get customer scripts into Redwood harness, decide streaming vs non-streaming approach for benchmark runs, agree on success criteria and acceptance tests, and align on timeline for a 3-week pilot.

Topics: workload sizing; script sanitization; KV cache warmup; batching vs continuous streaming; metrics and telemetry contract; security/PII handling; timeline and runbook.

--- Transcript body (auto) ---
[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have an hour plus to kick off. quick round robin?
[00:00:08] Liam: yeah, Liam here. short background — we're running ML inference for chatassist and product recs, about 1.2M monthly users, peak concurrent ~850 active sessions.
[00:00:25] Priya: priya — infra. we care about tail latency at 99.9, cold starts, and also the kv cash warmup pattern, we call it KV cash in our notes haha.
[00:00:35] Maya (Redwood SE): fair, we'll use the harness to reproduce the warmup. quick note: our harness supports both streaming responses and non-streaming (batch) ioctl — i mean mode.
[00:00:45] Carla: can you outline what you need from us to stitch our customer scripts in?
[00:00:50] Alex: sure. list is basically (1) representative prompt corpus, (2) traffic traces showing inter-arrival times, (3) example session length distribution, and (4) any session-specific KV keys that must be preserved.
[00:01:05] Daniel: we have a set of scripts — mostly node-based clients — we can sanitize a subset. question: do you need the browser-level streaming code or server-side wrappers?
[00:01:14] Jordan (Redwood): either works; for streaming latency profiling browser stubs are useful but we can emulate stream semantics server-side. important is end-to-end event timing.
[00:01:30] Speaker 3: (overlap) also what about quantization? is quan tiz ation part of the benchmark or later?
[00:01:37] Maya: we'll run baseline on float16/FP16 and then a quantized profile, yes — but primary pilot should be on your prod-like model variant.
[00:01:48] Liam: success criteria — for us it's twofold: 1) 95th and 99th p99 latency targets under peak load, and 2) cost per 1k requests delta vs current infra. we also want to ensure response quality doesn't degrade beyond a small threshold.
[00:02:05] Alex: can you define "small threshold" for quality?
[00:02:08] Carla: we use BLEU-ish and a business metric: drop in click-through on recs < 3% acceptable. also a qualitative pass from product.
[00:02:20] Maya: we'll set up eval suites tied to the prompt set so we can measure generation regressions automatically between model variants.
[00:02:35] Priya: security question: logs and transcripts — we need to ensure PII is stripped before being sent to any hosted endpoints. are you doing processing in our VPC for this pilot?
[00:02:45] Alex: for the POC we can run Redwood Dedicated in a private network — options: hosted with customer-managed VPC peering or Redwood Private instance. whichever you prefer for data handling.
[00:02:58] Liam: we'll prefer VPC peering for now. Daniel will own firewall and peering setup.
[00:03:05] Alex: noted.
[00:03:12] Maya: back to harness: two integration paths — adapter approach (you drop in a shim into your runtime that emits events to the harness) or script ingestion (we run your sanitized scripts inside harness runner). adapter gives closer fidelity to production, script ingestion is faster to onboard.
[00:03:30] Daniel: shim sounds safer for our telemetry but we'll need sample code for node.
[00:03:36] Alex: we'll supply node shim and a python example.
[00:03:40] Carla: timeline expectations?
[00:03:43] Alex: propose: week 1 (this week) — script handoff + peering; week 2 — harness integration + first non-streaming runs; week 3 — streaming runs, quant, and final acceptance. 3-week pilot.
[00:03:58] Liam: that speed is good. can you fit an initial smoke run earlier to validate configs?
[00:04:03] Maya: yes, we'll do a smoke test within 48 hours after scripts land.
[00:04:10] Speaker 2: (murmur)
[00:04:18] Alex: acceptance tests: defined SLOs for p95/p99, peak throughput sustain for 10 minutes, KV-cache warmup profile documented, and an automated quality regression check.
[00:04:30] Priya: metrics contract — we need token-level latency, per-request breakdown, per-model cost estimate and tail latency histograms and raw traces for a sample window.
[00:04:42] Maya: harness will emit prometheus-style metrics and also provide a CSV export; we'll share a sample dashboard.
[00:04:50] Liam: also please include per-route cost attribution.
[00:04:54] Jordan: sure.
[00:04:58] Carla: about streaming vs non-streaming — main worry is increased connection churn and proxy timeouts at our edge. do you have mitigations?
[00:05:07] Maya: we recommend continuous HTTP/2 streaming, connection pooling, and an autoscaler tuned to keep sessions warm. fallback is batch mode where we simulate streaming by slicing responses into chunks post-hoc — not ideal for latency but more predictable for infra.
[00:05:23] Daniel: in the batch-simulated streaming case, how do you model user-visible first-byte latency?
[00:05:28] Maya: we instrument first-token times in the harness and can replay those for user-observed metrics. we'll include first-byte and complete-response times.
[00:05:36] Liam: benchmarks: please include cold-start curves and steady-state throughput. we care about warmup behavior because our KV cache is session-scoped.
[00:05:46] Alex: agreed. also we'll run a tail-latency stress test with synthetic arrival bursts.
[00:05:52] Carla: how about failure scenarios? can the harness simulate model swap fallback?
[00:05:56] Maya: yes we support fault-injection: model surge, node OOMs, and network partition emulation. we'll show those in the demo.
[00:06:05] Priya: will you share a security pack — SOC 2 report, data flows, SSO support?
[00:06:10] Alex: yes, will attach security docs. also we have an NDA already in place but we'll re-confirm scope.
[00:06:18] Liam: one more — cost assumptions. we want a per-1k request cost estimate for the three candidate modes: hosted FP16, hosted quantized int8 (if available), and Dedicated reserved.
[00:06:30] Jordan: we'll produce an estimated cost model based on your traffic profile and model size.
[00:06:36] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[00:06:42] Alex: ok let me recap next steps — Alex to send harness onboarding + node shim; Maya to prepare streaming vs batch runbook and perf hypothesis; Priya to share traces; Liam to finalize success criteria matrix; schedule streaming deep-dive next Wednesday.
[00:06:58] Carla: sounds good. thanks all.
[00:07:02] Alex: thanks — end.

Artifacts shared during call: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/benchmark-spreadsheet-v2.xlsx (placeholder), shared drive folder: //nimble-shared/poctemp, node-shim repo link: https://git.redwood.internal/node-shim-sample (placeholder)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labels automatic, small mis-hearings like "K V cash" for "KV cache" and "quan tiz ation" for quantization; overall medium quality.

Acceptance criteria (restated):
- p95 and p99 targets per route (numbers to be filled once Liam shares target matrix)
- Tail latency behavior under 10-minute sustained peak window
- Quality regression < 3% business metric degradation + automated eval pass
- Successful streaming run without >=1% error rate for connections
- Security sign-off for data flows and peering configuration

End of transcript.
